title: AI Use and Verification
text:
AI system and date: ChatGPT, 11/9/2026

How is the amount spent on healthcare related to age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoking status, and region of the United States you live in? We are using a multiple linear regression model. The baseline result is that smoking, BMI, number of children, and age all are associated with significant changes in yearly healthcare charges. We wanted to see which predictors were the most important in predicting healthcare charges. Though we could use a best-subsets selection to get an idea of which matters most, we wanted to directly compare each variable’s importance on the same baseline. A model selection search will tell us which variables should be included, but not rank and measure their importance.

Accepted: We used ChatGPT’s advice for what extension may work well. We used most of the advice it had for implementation and the code it gave us to create the permutation importance feature. We used the graphic and simulation it made to create the permutation feature.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Independent verification

If our extension shows that smoking, age, and BMI are substantially more important than the other predictors, than a best-subsets selection using BIC should hopefully select those same predictors.



Show code
bestglm::bestglm(
    insurance_data |> select(-bmi_group) |> as.data.frame(), 
    TopModels = 5,
    IC = "BIC"
)$BestModels


   age   sex  bmi children smoker region Criterion
1 TRUE FALSE TRUE     TRUE   TRUE  FALSE  23333.75
2 TRUE FALSE TRUE    FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  23338.35
3 TRUE  TRUE TRUE     TRUE   TRUE  FALSE  23340.80
4 TRUE  TRUE TRUE    FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  23345.45
5 TRUE FALSE TRUE     TRUE   TRUE   TRUE  23348.98



This best-subsets BIC selection selects age, bmi, children, and smoker. This is some weak evidence that the AI’s importance ranking is correct, as these are the top 4 predictors, but this best-subsets search does not rank the predictors in any way. This is why a best-subsets selection or other model selection method is not sufficient for ranking the importance of predictors, because the only information we get is if a variable should be included or not, whereas the AI’s importance ranking assigns values to each predictor which we can use to rank and compare them. Because we only get a TRUE or FALSE for each predictor, we cannot say which matters most for prediction with a normal model selection search algorithm.


We can use \(R^2\) to explore which variables are the most important. We can fit partial models, each one dropping one of our predictors, and see how much the \(R^2\) decreases when we drop each variable.



Show code
partial1 <- lm(charges ~ . - age - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial2 <- lm(charges ~ . - sex - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial3 <- lm(charges ~ . - bmi - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial4 <- lm(charges ~ . - children - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial5 <- lm(charges ~ . - smoker - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial6 <- lm(charges ~ . - region - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)

adj.r.squareds <- c(
    glance(partial1)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial2)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial3)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial4)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial5)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial6)$adj.r.squared
)

results.chart <- tibble(
    `Dropped Predictor` = c("Age", "Sex", "BMI", "Children", "Smoker", "Region"),
    `Drop in adjusted R^2` = glance(insurance_fit)$adj.r.squared - adj.r.squareds
) |> arrange(desc(`Drop in adjusted R^2`))

This table lists the change in adjusted \(R^2\), where a positive number means a drop in adjusted \(R^2\). Omitting each of the variables caused a drop in adjusted \(R^2\) except for sex, however the drop due to omitting region, children, and sex were all very small (<.003). This also reinforces the AI work, showing that age, BMI, and especially smoking status have a significant impact on the accuracy of the predictions. \(R^2\) is also nice because it is quantifiable. The change in \(R^2\) is the change in the percentage of variation that the model explains when we add that predictor. So, we can see that removing smoker causes the amount of variation explained to drop by nearly 63%, removing age and bmi cause the amount of explained variation to drop by about 9% and 3% respectively, while removing sex, children, or region cause a drop of less than .3% each, or even an increase in the case of sex.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Remaining limitation
One limitation that remains is that that correlation does not mean causation. We’re modeling the impact of sex, children, smoker, BMI, age, and region, but there are other factors that could be impacting insurance pricing that the data doesn’t show. An example of this could be previous medical history or disabilities that can influence the price. Even though the permutation importance simulation, the best-subsets selection using BIC, and the drop in \(R^2\) all show that smoker can explain a lot of the variation in healthcare charges, we cannot conclude that healthcare charges are increased by smoking.

title: Health Insurance Pricing
text:
The question
In one or two short paragraphs, introduce the setting, audience, focused research question, data source, observational unit, response, important predictors, and one important data limitation. Lead with what makes the question worth answering.
How is the amount spent on healthcare related to age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoking status, and region of the United States you life in? This study is for those setting health insurance pricing so that they can better understand the effect of these factors on the amount of health insurance a policyholder will need. Understanding these relationships can help insurance companies make more informed decisions when determining insurance premiums and help policyholders identify factors associated with higher healthcare costs. The data comes from the insurance.csv dataset, originally published in Brett Lantz’s Machine Learning with R and available through Kaggle. The observational unit is one individual, with a total of 1,338 individuals and seven variables. The response variable is charges, which represents the total annual healthcare charges for each individual. The six candidate predictors are age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, and region.
We expect smoking status to be one of the strongest predictors of healthcare charges, with age and BMI also likely to have important associations. Identifying these relationships may help insurance companies better understand healthcare costs when setting premiums and help policyholders recognize factors associated with higher insurance expenses. However, an important limitation is that the dataset is observational and provides limited information about its original data collection process. Therefore, we can identify associations between these variables and healthcare charges, but we cannot conclude that any of these factors directly cause healthcare costs to increase or decrease.

It is clear from these plots that healthcare charges increase with age, and that smokers generally spend more per year for healthcare. BMI doesn’t seem to have as much of an effect as expected, however it seems to have an interaction with smoking status. Healthcare costs seem to stay mostly the same as BMI increases except for the group of individuals who are smokers and obese. Smokers in the normal and overweight BMI categories seem to be charged about $15000 more per year across the age levels recorded, but obese smokers are charged about $35000 more on average across all age levels.

title: Health Insurance Pricing
text:
A new direction with AI
We want to decide which predictors impact the predictions of healthcare charges the most. We are going to use ask AI about the best way to make this comparison. It returned a method of ranking each predictor and assigning them levels of importance by randomly permuting each variable and checking to see how much the cross validated RMSE changes. This procedure will extend what our LASSO regression found, by hopefully confirming which the most important variables are, but also by giving each predictor a measure of importance in the same units. This will show us how strongly each of our predictors is related to healthcare charges. To check this work, we will also fit a BIC best-subsets model because it should select the same predictors if they are truly the most important. We will also compare the \(R^2\) values for the full baseline model to the \(R^2\) from models with all of the predictors except one. If the variables found to be the most important by the AI’s simulation are truly the most important, then the drop in \(R^2\) should be the largest for the most important predictors.


Show code
# Implement the verified extension or show its most useful result.

library(tidymodels)

set.seed(502340)

folds <- vfold_cv(
  insurance_data,
  v = 10,
  repeats = 5
)

# Predictors to investigate
predictors <- c(
  "age",
  "sex",
  "bmi",
  "children",
  "smoker",
  "region"
)

# Number of random permutations
n_permutations <- 30

# Calculate permutation importance

importance_results <- map2_dfr(
  folds$splits,
  seq_along(folds$splits),

  function(split, i) {

    # Separate training and assessment observations
    train_data <- analysis(split)
    test_data <- assessment(split)

    # Fit regression using training observations
    model <- lm(
      charges ~ age + sex + bmi +
        children + smoker + region,
      data = train_data
    )

    # Original predictions and RMSE
    original_predictions <- predict(
      model,
      newdata = test_data
    )

    original_rmse <- rmse_vec(
      truth = test_data$charges,
      estimate = original_predictions
    )

    # Shuffle each predictor independently
    map_dfr(
      predictors,

      function(variable) {

        shuffled_rmse <- replicate(
          n_permutations,

          {
            shuffled_data <- test_data

            shuffled_data[[variable]] <-
              sample(shuffled_data[[variable]])

            predictions <- predict(
              model,
              newdata = shuffled_data
            )

            rmse_vec(
              truth = test_data$charges,
              estimate = predictions
            )
          }
        )

        tibble(
          fold = folds$id[i],
          repeat_id = folds$id2[i],
          variable = variable,
          original_rmse = original_rmse,
          permutation = seq_len(n_permutations),
          shuffled_rmse = shuffled_rmse,
          importance = shuffled_rmse - original_rmse
        )
      }
    )
  }
)


importance_summary <- importance_results %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_importance = mean(importance),
    sd_importance = sd(importance),
    median_importance = median(importance),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_importance))
